table.text: The institutional Research Ethics Board approved this study.
Participants were between the ages of 18 and 29 (M = 20.03, SD = 2.74).
Participants provided informed consent before completing all procedures.
Participants were first screened to determine eligibility.
Participants were asked whether they experienced thoughts of killing themselves in the past year and whether they had an aborted attempt, interrupted attempt, or suicide attempt in the past year.
As part of safety protocols, participants provided contact information for someone close to them.
Eligible participants completed two baseline appointments that included clinical interviews, questionnaires, and computerized tasks prior to beginning the three-week (21-day) EMA period.
All participants were remunerated with gift cards.
Participants had 60 minutes to complete each survey.
Participants completed baseline questionnaires and responded to items pertaining to momentary defeat, entrapment, and SI at each EMA prompt.
At baseline, participants completed a demographics questionnaire designed for the study.
Sample size was determined by the number of eligible participants recruited during the study period; we recruited as many as we could with available funding.
Participants were young adults with a recent history of suicidal thoughts or behaviours, recruited from a university study pool and the broader community in Eastern Ontario, Canada.
Are participants were predominantly women and White, although several other gender and racial or ethnic groups were represented.
Participants were, on average, 20.03 years old (SD = 2.74, range = 18-29).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: DEFEAT, ENTRAPMENT, AND SUICIDAL IDEATION
keywords: CRediT Author Contributions Neha Parvez: Conceptualization
Writing -review & editing. Emilia Sherifi: Data curation

text.text: The Integrated Motivational-Volitional (IMV) model of suicide proposes that feelings of defeat give rise to entrapment, which in turn contributes to suicidal ideation (SI).
Although research generally supports this pathway, less is understood about how defeat, entrapment, and SI mutually influence each other over short periods of time.

Within a three-week ecological momentary assessment period, we examined short-term temporal associations among defeat, entrapment, and SI (passive and active) in a sample of young adults (N = 156, ages 18-29; data collected 2022-2023) with a recent history of suicidal thoughts or behaviours.
We used residual dynamic structural equation models to test concurrent and prospective within-person associations among variables.
Higher-than-usual levels of defeat and entrapment were each associated with greater passive and active SI at the same assessment and predicted greater SI at the subsequent assessment.
Defeat and entrapment also demonstrated reciprocal associations over time, such that greater levels of each predicted subsequent increases in the other.
Similarly, higher-thanusual levels of passive SI predicted subsequent increases in both defeat and entrapment, whereas active SI predicted subsequent increases in defeat only.
Findings support the central role of defeat and entrapment in short-term changes in SI.
Further, they suggest that the relationship between defeat and entrapment may be reciprocal rather than strictly unidirectional, challenging assumptions of the IMV model.
The generalizability of these findings to other age groups and clinical populations remains to be established.
Feelings of defeat and entrapment are thought to contribute to suicidal thinking.

This study found that feelings of being defeated and trapped uniquely and separately predicted increases in suicidal thoughts over the following hours and increases in either experience also predicted subsequent increases in the other.

Suicidal thoughts, particularly wishes to die, also predicted increases in feelings of defeat and entrapment, suggesting that these experiences may contribute to a self-reinforcing cycle of distress rather than effects being unidirectional and sequential.
Suicidal ideation (SI), broadly defined as thoughts about ending one's own life, is prevalent and often precedes suicidal behaviour (Nock et al., 2008b).
text.formatted: Suicidal ideation (SI), broadly defined as thoughts about ending one's own life, is prevalent and often precedes suicidal behaviour <ref type="bibr">(Nock et al., 2008b)</ref>.

text.text: Among youth, suicide is a leading cause of death worldwide, and rates may be increasing in some demographics (WHO, 2021).
text.formatted: Among youth, suicide is a leading cause of death worldwide, and rates may be increasing in some demographics <ref type="bibr">(WHO, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: While suicide is complex and difficult to predict (Franklin et al., 2017), several ideationto-action theories have described processes that lead to the emergence of SI and subsequent transition to suicidal behaviour.
text.formatted: While suicide is complex and difficult to predict <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Franklin et al., 2017)</ref>, several ideationto-action theories have described processes that lead to the emergence of SI and subsequent transition to suicidal behaviour.

text.text: The Integrated Motivational-Volitional model (IMV model; O'Connor, 2011; O'Connor & Kirtley, 2018) is a three-phase framework that explains why SI first onsets and how it escalates to suicidal behaviour.
text.formatted: The Integrated Motivational-Volitional model (IMV model; <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">O'Connor, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">O'Connor & Kirtley, 2018)</ref> is a three-phase framework that explains why SI first onsets and how it escalates to suicidal behaviour.

text.text: In the pre-motivational phase, background factors and triggering events heighten vulnerability to suicidal thoughts and behaviours.
The motivational phase, germane to this study, describes the emergence of SI.

Specifically, experiences of defeat (i.e., failed struggle) are thought to give rise to feelings of entrapment (i.e., a perceived inability to escape an aversive situation), which in turn contribute to SI.
Entrapment is therefore theorized to be a proximal driver of suicidal thinking.

Finally, the volitional phase describes the transition from ideation to suicidal behaviour, which is influenced by factors such as capability for suicide, access to lethal means, exposure to suicidal behaviour, and planning and preparatory behaviours.
The IMV model is particularly useful for understanding the emergence of SI because it organizes multiple risk factors within a cohesive framework while insinuating multiple distinct pathways to SI.

That is, individuals may experience different background vulnerabilities and triggering events, but these experiences are theorized to contribute to SI through the proximal processes of defeat and entrapment (O'Connor & Kirtley, 2018).
text.formatted: That is, individuals may experience different background vulnerabilities and triggering events, but these experiences are theorized to contribute to SI through the proximal processes of defeat and entrapment <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(O'Connor & Kirtley, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The model is also appropriate for understanding suicidal experiences on timescales in which they change (i.e., hours or days; Kleiman et al., 2017; Sherifi et al., 2026).
text.formatted: The model is also appropriate for understanding suicidal experiences on timescales in which they change (i.e., hours or days; <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Kleiman et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Sherifi et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The IMV focuses on near-term contributors to suicide outcomes that may meaningfully fluctuate in shorter timescales.
The motivational phase of the IMV model has considerable empirical support.
Several studies have found concurrent positive associations among defeat, entrapment, and SI ( O'Connor & Kirtley, 2018; Souza et al., 2024; Taylor et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Several studies have found concurrent positive associations among defeat, entrapment, and SI ( <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">O'Connor & Kirtley, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Souza et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Taylor et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Entrapment mediates associations between earlier defeat and subsequent SI in longitudinal studies, in line with the IMV's hypotheses (Branley-Bell et al., 2019; Wetherall et al., 2022; Xiao et al., 2026).

text.text: However, other studies do not find these proposed pathways (Souza et al., 2024).
text.formatted: However, other studies do not find these proposed pathways <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Souza et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Extant longitudinal research has measured IMV constructs over weeks or months and thus cannot address whether these variables contribute to short-term (i.e., within hours or days) changes in SI in the manner the theory proposes.

SI can vary considerably within hours and days (Kleiman et al., 2017; Nock et al., 2009) and cognitive or affective states may drive rapid increases (e.g., Kivelä et al., 2024; Scott & Brown, 2025; Rath et al., 2019).
text.formatted: SI can vary considerably within hours and days <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Kleiman et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Nock et al., 2009)</ref> and cognitive or affective states may drive rapid increases (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Kivelä et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Scott & Brown, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Rath et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Defeat and entrapment may also be cognitive-affective states that are not stable, even over short time periods.

Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA), a tool for repeatedly assessing people in their natural environments, may therefore be well suited to examining the short-term, within-person relationships between defeat, entrapment, and SI.

Emerging EMA research partially supports the IMV but also suggests that the relations between defeat, entrapment and SI are more complex than the linear sequence the model proposes. Stenzel and colleagues (2020) found high within-person variability in defeat and entrapment and a concurrent association between the two constructs.

text.text: However, defeat did not predict entrapment at the subsequent assessment approximately two hours later.

Van Ballegooijen and colleagues (2022) examined defeat, entrapment, and SI among adults with recent suicidal thoughts or behaviours and found that entrapment was associated with SI both concurrently and prospectively.

Further, they found reciprocal temporal associations between defeat and entrapment at approximately three-hour prompt intervals. Moscardini and colleagues (2023) found that defeat predicted entrapment only concurrently, whereas entrapment predicted suicidal desire both concurrently and prospectively.

text.text: Together, these findings suggest that entrapment is particularly relevant to subsequent changes in suicidal thinking, but it is less clear how defeat and entrapment covary in short time windows.

A recent review of EMA research examining IMV constructs found evidence for both concurrent and lagged associations between entrapment and self-harm thoughts and behaviours but highlighted the limited and methodologically heterogeneous nature of this literature (Winstone et al., 2024).

text.text: Another consideration is that SI encompasses a range of cognitions that vary in explicit content.

Although the distinction between passive and active SI is inconsistent in the literature, one common characterization has been that passive SI is a desire or wish to die, whereas active SI involves explicit thoughts of killing oneself (e.g., Van Orden et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Although the distinction between passive and active SI is inconsistent in the literature, one common characterization has been that passive SI is a desire or wish to die, whereas active SI involves explicit thoughts of killing oneself (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Van Orden et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Across two large samples of adults, Wastler and colleagues (2023) found that passive and active suicidal thoughts were better represented as two related constructs (i.e., generally described as thoughts reflecting a desire for death or nonexistence, and thoughts explicitly involving killing oneself) rather than as a single construct with varying "gradients" or degrees of severity.

text.text: Although some ideation-toaction theories of suicide propose a progression from less to more severe forms of suicidal thinking, with active SI occurring later and more proximally to suicidal behaviour (e.g., Klonsky & May, 2015; Van Orden et al., 2010), passive SI may not simply represent an earlier or less severe cognitive state.

text.text: For example, a meta-analysis of 86 studies found that passive SI was associated with suicide attempts and other established correlates of suicide risk, with largely similar correlates observed for passive and active SI (Liu et al., 2020).

text.text: Moreover, some individuals with a history of suicide attempts report passive SI without ever experiencing active SI (Wastler et al., 2022), suggesting that suicidal thoughts and behaviours may not always follow a progression from passive to active SI.

text.text: Research on passive and active SI highlights the importance of considering variability in SI content.

Examining passive and active SI separately may therefore provide a more nuanced understanding of whether factors associated with SI operate similarly across distinct forms of ideation (e.g., thoughts of death versus thoughts of killing oneself).
However, existing EMA research on defeat and entrapment has generally not distinguished between passive and active SI, particularly regarding temporal associations with defeat and entrapment.
For example, van Ballegooijen et al. (2022) assessed temporal associations between defeat, entrapment, and SI, but SI was assessed using a single item ("Right now, I feel suicidal").
text.formatted: For example, van <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Ballegooijen et al. (2022)</ref> assessed temporal associations between defeat, entrapment, and SI, but SI was assessed using a single item ("Right now, I feel suicidal").

text.text: Consequently, it remains unclear whether defeat and entrapment contribute similarly to short-term fluctuations in passive and active SI.

This distinction has implications for suicide theories that propose separate contributors to passive and active SI (e.g., Klonsky & May, 2015; Van Orden et al., 2010) and generally for understanding how suicidal thoughts may escalate or worsen in some cases.
text.formatted: This distinction has implications for suicide theories that propose separate contributors to passive and active SI (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Klonsky & May, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Van Orden et al., 2010)</ref> and generally for understanding how suicidal thoughts may escalate or worsen in some cases.

text.text: Taken together, gaps in our understanding of short-term changes in SI highlight the need for further intensive longitudinal research examining momentary associations among defeat, entrapment, and SI, attending to the latter's content.
Clarifying the temporal sequence among these variables has implications beyond evaluating the IMV model.
For example, if defeat precedes increases in entrapment, defeat might be an earlier, potentially actionable indicator of an unfolding process associated with SI.
Alternatively, if entrapment is more proximally associated with subsequent SI, increases in entrapment may signal a point at which SI is more likely to emerge or intensify.
Defeat and entrapment may also be independently associated with subsequent SI, rather than operating primarily through the sequential pathway proposed by the IMV model.
This would raise the possibility that defeat and entrapment are part of distinct pathways to suicidal thinking.
Consequently, such findings would indicate that defeat and entrapment should be investigated separately.

This would challenge the notion that defeat and entrapment reflect the same general construct (Griffiths et al., 2015; Taylor et al., 2009), despite how they are described in the IMV model (O'Connor & Kirtley, 2018).

text.text: Examining these processes may be particularly important among young adults, given the high prevalence of suicidal thoughts and behaviours during this developmental period (Han et al., 2016; Nock et al., 2008a Nock et al., , 2008b)).

text.text: Ultimately, establishing how defeat and entrapment contribute to SI over short timescales may help identify clinically meaningful changes in risk, and that could be viable targets for intervention.

We used a three-week EMA protocol to examine the short-term, within-person associations between defeat, entrapment, and both passive and active SI in a community-based sample of young adults with past-year SI and/or suicide attempt.

We examine whether momentary changes in defeat and entrapment are associated with passive and active SI concurrently and prospectively at the subsequent assessment, as well as the prospective associations between defeat and entrapment.

In line with prior research and theory, we hypothesize that within-person increases in defeat and entrapment will be associated with greater passive and active SI at the same timepoint, and that increases in entrapment will predict greater passive and active SI at the subsequent assessment.
Given mixed findings regarding the shortterm temporal relationship between defeat and entrapment, we examine their prospective associations without a directional hypothesis.
Participants (N = 156) were young adults with a history of SI or attempt recruited from an undergraduate study pool and the broader community in a city in Eastern Ontario, Canada.
Participants were between the ages of 18 and 29 (M = 20.03, SD = 2.74).

text.text: Momentary SI was assessed using two items capturing passive and active ideation.
Passive SI was assessed with the item, "Right now, how strong is your desire/wish to die," rated on a scale from 0 ("not at all") to 100 ("very much").
Active SI was assessed with the item "Right now, how intense is your desire/wish to kill yourself", rated on a scale from 0 ("absent/no intent") to 9 ("extremely strong").

Items measuring momentary defeat (two items) and entrapment (two items) were adapted from the Short Defeat and Entrapment Scale (SDES; Griffiths et al., 2015), an 8-item self-report measure with excellent internal consistency.

text.text: Participants responded to items on a visual analogue slider scale ranging from 0 ("not at all") to 100 ("very much").
Items for defeat were "at this moment, I feel…defeated by life" and "…I feel powerless".
Items for entrapment were "…like getting away from who I am and starting again" and "…like there is no way out of my current situation".
Average scores for defeat and entrapment using each of the two items were computed.
We used Residual Dynamic Structural Equation Modelling (RDSEM) to examine the temporal relationships between entrapment, defeat, and both passive and active suicidal ideation.

DSEM extends multilevel structural equation modelling by explicitly modelling the temporal ordering of observations, making it particularly well suited for analyzing lagged within-person processes (McNeish & Hamaker, 2020).
text.formatted: DSEM extends multilevel structural equation modelling by explicitly modelling the temporal ordering of observations, making it particularly well suited for analyzing lagged within-person processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(McNeish & Hamaker, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Within RDSEM, the multilevel structure separates within-person dynamics from between-person differences.
The within-person level captures how variables change over time within individuals, whereas the between-person level examines stable differences between individuals.
The cross-lagged panel models used included both autoregressive and cross-lagged effects.
Autoregressive paths quantify inertia by estimating the extent to which a variable at one assessment predicts itself at the subsequent assessment.
Cross-lagged paths estimate whether changes in one variable predict subsequent changes in another variable over time.
Random effects were specified for intercepts, autoregressive and cross-lagged slopes, and residual variances, allowing these parameters to vary across individuals.
This accounts for betweenperson differences in average levels of each construct, the strength of temporal associations, and the amount of unexplained within-person variability.
In each model, we included time as a covariate to account for trends in the outcome (i.e., tendencies for increases or decreases in wish to die over the course of the study).

We estimated DSEM using Bayesian methods, which are required for this modelling framework and facilitate the estimation of complex models while providing robust handling of missing data (Asparouhov, Hamaker, & Muthén, 2018).
text.formatted: We estimated DSEM using Bayesian methods, which are required for this modelling framework and facilitate the estimation of complex models while providing robust handling of missing data <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Asparouhov, Hamaker, & Muthén, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Standardized parameter estimates were interpreted alongside their 95% credibility intervals, which represent the range within which the true parameter is estimated to lie with 95% probability.
Effects were considered statistically significant when the corresponding credibility interval did not include zero.
DSEM assumes equally spaced observations when estimating temporal associations.
However, EMA data commonly contain irregular spacing due to overnight intervals, missed reports, and semi-random prompt timing.

To account for these irregular intervals, the TINTERVAL function in Mplus was used to create a time variable based on three-hour intervals, inserting missing data records where observations were misaligned (Asparouhov, Hamaker, & Muthén, 2018).

text.text: Model convergence was evaluated using the Potential Scale Reduction (PSR) statistic, with values close to 1.00 indicating adequate convergence by demonstrating minimal between-chain variability relative to total variability (Muthén, 2010).

text.text: Trace plots were also visually inspected for evidence of poor convergence, including non-random patterns and autocorrelation between draws, with no abnormalities observed.
To minimize the risk of premature convergence, the number of iterations was increased until PSR values stabilized.
Each model was estimated using 10,000 iterations with a thinning interval of 10.

Finally, all withinperson variables were modelled as latent person-mean centred, which improves the interpretability of within-person effects and reduces Nickell's bias when estimating autoregressive parameters.

Our goal was to examine short-term associations among defeat, entrapment, and SI and test hypotheses grounded in the IMV model of suicide (O'Connor & Kirtley, 2018).

text.text: Several key findings emerged.
First, defeat and entrapment were concurrently associated with both passive and active SI.
Second, within-person increases in both defeat and entrapment prospectively predicted increases in SI (passive and active) at the next assessment.

Third, defeat and entrapment were reciprocally associated across time; higher-than-usual levels of defeat predicted subsequent increases in entrapment, consistent with the IMV model, but higher-than-usual entrapment also predicted subsequent defeat.
Finally, within-person increases in passive SI reciprocally predicted both defeat and entrapment, but active SI only predicted subsequent defeat, and not entrapment.
Together, these findings highlight the importance of defeat and entrapment in understanding short-term fluctuations in suicidal thinking.
They suggest that the temporal relationships among IMV constructs are more dynamic and reciprocal than the model proposes.
Consistent with prior research, defeat and entrapment were concurrently associated with passive and active SI.

Importantly, these associations were at the within-person level; at moments when individuals experienced greater defeat or entrapment relative to their own typical levels, they also reported more severe SI.

These findings extend evidence from traditional crosssectional research by demonstrating that associations among defeat, entrapment, and SI are also evident in fluctuations occurring within individuals in daily life.
They also demonstrate the value of assessing these variables repeatedly in situ.

This distinction is important because betweenperson associations (e.g., that individuals who generally report greater entrapment also report greater SI) do not necessarily indicate that increases in entrapment within a given individual would forecast changes in that same person's SI.
Our results further suggest that defeat and entrapment are relevant to understanding momentary changes in forms of SI with distinct thought content.
Passive and active SI are related but distinguishable types of suicide cognition, and not different locations on a spectrum of severity (Wastler et al., 2023).

text.text: Our findings highlight the value of considering both the dynamics and content of suicidal thinking.
They also contribute to a growing body of literature focused on understanding whether predictors have differential short-term effects on passive versus active SI.
Prior intensive longitudinal research suggests that such distinctions may be meaningful.

For example, some components of sleep disturbance have shown different within-person associations with passive and active SI (Cox et al., 2023), while daily sleepiness may influence the strength of the association between the two forms of SI (Porter & Bishop, 2024).

text.text: Thus, the present findings support continued examination of the distinct forms of SI when examining proximal correlates.
In the IMV model, entrapment is a proximal driver of suicidal ideation (O'Connor & Kirtley, 2018).

text.text: Our findings support this theoretical assumption and align with prior EMA research (Moscardini et al., 2023; van Ballegooijen et al., 2022).

text.text: However, in contrast to van Ballegooijen and colleagues (2022), we found that defeat also predicted subsequent active and passive SI.
Importantly, our findings suggest that the short-term relevance of defeat may not be limited to its proposed role as an antecedent to entrapment.
Rather, elevations in both defeat and entrapment may signal proximal increases in SI over the ensuing hours.
In daily life, the worsening of SI may be driven by dynamic relationships among defeat and entrapment, rather than entrapment alone.

Defeat and entrapment may be associated with subsequent SI through their mutual effects on other putative near-term predictors like hopelessness, which has been associated with SI in prior EMA research (see Kleiman et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Defeat and entrapment may be associated with subsequent SI through their mutual effects on other putative near-term predictors like hopelessness, which has been associated with SI in prior EMA research (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Kleiman et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Defeat and entrapment involve perceiving adversity as insurmountable.

This is consistent with the emphasis on hopelessness in the Interpersonal Theory of Suicide (Van Orden et al., 2010), which proposes that hopelessness about changing adverse interpersonal circumstances contributes to the desire to die.
text.formatted: This is consistent with the emphasis on hopelessness in the Interpersonal Theory of Suicide <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Van Orden et al., 2010)</ref>, which proposes that hopelessness about changing adverse interpersonal circumstances contributes to the desire to die.

text.text: Further, defeat and entrapment may reflect a common underlying construct (Griffiths et al., 2015) but are also theorized to be distinct (O'Connor & Kirtley, 2018).
text.formatted: Further, defeat and entrapment may reflect a common underlying construct <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Griffiths et al., 2015)</ref> but are also theorized to be distinct <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(O'Connor & Kirtley, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Further research is needed on the construct validity of defeat and entrapment measured in EMA studies.

Additionally, future studies should examine likely mediators of the effects of entrapment and defeat on subsequent short-term changes in SI (e.g., hopelessness) to understand discrepancies between findings like ours and the IMV's predictions.
We also found reciprocal prospective associations between defeat and entrapment, providing partial support for the temporal ordering the IMV model proposes.
We found that moments of greater defeat predicted subsequent increases in entrapment.
However, greater entrapment also predicted subsequent increases in defeat, and this prospective link is not explicitly hypothesized by the IMV.
Bidirectional effects between these variables replicate prior findings in studies that also considered relatively short measurement intervals (van Ballegooijen et al.,2022).
text.formatted: Bidirectional effects between these variables replicate prior findings in studies that also considered relatively short measurement intervals <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(van Ballegooijen et al.,2022)</ref>.

text.text: We extended this work by examining these processes in relation to passive and active SI separately.

Some recent EMA research has found that predictors of passive and active SI do not completely overlap (e.g., Hallensleben et al., 2019; Weires et al., 2025), and we add to a growing literature on this issue.
text.formatted: Some recent EMA research has found that predictors of passive and active SI do not completely overlap (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Hallensleben et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Weires et al., 2025)</ref>, and we add to a growing literature on this issue.

text.text: Ultimately, determining shared versus distinct drivers of these forms of SI has important clinical implications, which we discuss below.
We contend that the related but separable states of defeat and entrapment reinforce one another.

Consistent with the IMV model, repeated experiences of unsuccessful struggle may contribute to perceptions of entrapment, an interpretation that aligns with research demonstrating the effects of uncontrollable aversive experiences on subsequent escape behaviour (Maier & Seligman, 2016).
text.formatted: Consistent with the IMV model, repeated experiences of unsuccessful struggle may contribute to perceptions of entrapment, an interpretation that aligns with research demonstrating the effects of uncontrollable aversive experiences on subsequent escape behaviour <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Maier & Seligman, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, feeling trapped may activate or strengthen negative beliefs about oneself and one's ability to overcome adversity, such that subsequent difficulties are increasingly interpreted as evidence of personal failure.
This is consistent with theories of suicide that emphasize the activation of suicidogenic schemas thought to precede suicidal crises (Rudd, 2006; Wenzel & Beck, 2008).
text.formatted: This is consistent with theories of suicide that emphasize the activation of suicidogenic schemas thought to precede suicidal crises <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Rudd, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Wenzel & Beck, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: In short timescales, the transactional, mutually-reinforcing relations between defeat, entrapment and SI may acutely escalate the severity of suicidal thinking.
However, these relations may be specific to the within-day level and not detected when assessments are spaced further apart.

Over longer timeframes, effects may be unidirectional and sequential as the IMV insinuates (O'Connor & Kirtley, 2018) and some studies find (Branley-Bell et al., 2019; Wetherall et al., 2022; Xiao et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Over longer timeframes, effects may be unidirectional and sequential as the IMV insinuates <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(O'Connor & Kirtley, 2018)</ref> and some studies find <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Branley-Bell et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Wetherall et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Xiao et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Overall, suicide theories must continue to be examined at different timescales and potentially revised to describe the shorterversus longer-term effects of key variables.
Our findings further suggest that the reciprocal dynamics between defeat and entrapment may extend to suicidal thinking itself, although this pattern was different for passive versus active SI.
Passive SI predicted subsequent defeat and entrapment, but active SI only predicted subsequent defeat.

However, the association between active SI and subsequent defeat was no longer statistically significant when participants with no within-person variability in SI were removed (see Supplementary Tables S1-S3); thus, the finding warrants cautious interpretation and further investigation.
text.formatted: However, the association between active SI and subsequent defeat was no longer statistically significant when participants with no within-person variability in SI were removed (see Supplementary Tables <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">S1-S3</ref>); thus, the finding warrants cautious interpretation and further investigation.

text.text: One possible explanation for the dissociation between passive and active SI effects is that people who endorse active SI may view suicide as a viable way to end their current state (see Al-Dajani et al., 2019).
text.formatted: One possible explanation for the dissociation between passive and active SI effects is that people who endorse active SI may view suicide as a viable way to end their current state (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Al-Dajani et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: At its core, entrapment is characterized by the perception of being trapped in an aversive situation from which escape is perceived as unavailable; while some people with active SI may feel stuck, suicide may seem like a way to become "unstuck" for others, collectively weakening the connection between active SI and entrapment.
In contrast, our passive SI item inquired about a desire or wish to die.

In recent latent class analyses of suicide content, classes characterized predominantly by passive SI items lacked endorsement of items referring to suicide planning and preparatory actions (Martin et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In recent latent class analyses of suicide content, classes characterized predominantly by passive SI items lacked endorsement of items referring to suicide planning and preparatory actions <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Martin et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: People endorsing primarily passive SI may experience less escape-related cognition; the anguish related to their passive SI may therefore increase subsequent feelings of entrapment.
However, our interpretation is speculative, particularly because we did not directly assess whether suicide was perceived as a means of escape.
Our findings also have implications for the assessment and treatment of suicidal thinking.
Defeat and entrapment may be important constructs to monitor in practice given that withinperson elevations in entrapment preceded increases in both passive and active SI.
Put another way, changes relative to a person's typical level of defeat and entrapment may be clinically informative, even beyond the absolute severity of these states.

This idea is consistent with interventions for suicide such as the Safety Planning Intervention (Stanley & Brown, 2012), which emphasizes identifying individualized warning signs of an emerging suicidal crisis and linking these warning signs with coping strategies, sources of support, and other steps that can be implemented as risk increases.
text.formatted: This idea is consistent with interventions for suicide such as the Safety Planning Intervention <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Stanley & Brown, 2012)</ref>, which emphasizes identifying individualized warning signs of an emerging suicidal crisis and linking these warning signs with coping strategies, sources of support, and other steps that can be implemented as risk increases.

text.text: Future research is needed to d etermine whether increases in defeat and/or entrapment may be individualized warning signs and whether monitoring within-person changes in these constructs provides actionable information beyond what is obtained in existing suicide risk assessments.
Elevated defeat and entrapment may also be useful as a signal that further assessment is needed.
Elevated entrapment suggests someone feels stuck in an aversive situation but does not identify the circumstances producing that perception.

These circumstances may be interpersonal (e.g., relationship conflict, social isolation), intrapersonal (e.g., difficulty coping, distressing thoughts or emotions), or situational (e.g., stressors in various domains of life) and are likely to require different clinical responses (O'Connor & Kirtley, 2018).
text.formatted: These circumstances may be interpersonal (e.g., relationship conflict, social isolation), intrapersonal (e.g., difficulty coping, distressing thoughts or emotions), or situational (e.g., stressors in various domains of life) and are likely to require different clinical responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(O'Connor & Kirtley, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, identifying elevated entrapment may provide an opportunity to explore what is contributing to a patient's SI and general despair.

For example, entrapment arising from social isolation may require a different response than entrapment arising from interpersonal conflict, academic or occupational difficulties, or difficulty managing distressing internal experiences.
The prospective associations do not indicate that elevated defeat and entrapment alone are a marker of imminent suicide risk in all cases.

Suicidal thinking is influenced by multiple interpersonal, affective, cognitive, and contextual processes (Franklin et al., 2017; O'Connor & Kirtley, 2018), and the present study examined only a subset of these factors.
text.formatted: Suicidal thinking is influenced by multiple interpersonal, affective, cognitive, and contextual processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Franklin et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">O'Connor & Kirtley, 2018)</ref>, and the present study examined only a subset of these factors.

text.text: An important next step will therefore be to determine whether momentary entrapment provides unique information about subsequent changes in SI when considered alongside other dynamic factors.

Intensive longitudinal studies incorporating constructs across multiple theoretical frameworks could help establish the incremental contribution of entrapment and identify combinations of experiences that are particularly relevant to short-term changes in SI.
Such work may ultimately clarify whether monitoring changes in entrapment can contribute meaningfully to individualized approaches to assessing and responding to suicidal thinking.
Lastly, our results contribute to a growing body of research suggesting that passive SI warrants careful assessment and structured intervention in clinical practice.

Historically, passive SI has received comparatively less research and clinical attention than active SI, potentially reflecting assumptions that wishes for death represent a less concerning form of suicidal thinking (Liu et al., 2020; Szanto et al., 1996).
text.formatted: Historically, passive SI has received comparatively less research and clinical attention than active SI, potentially reflecting assumptions that wishes for death represent a less concerning form of suicidal thinking <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Liu et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Szanto et al., 1996)</ref>.

text.text: However, a systematic review and meta-analysis found that passive and active SI share largely comparable clinical and psychological correlates, including associations with suicide attempts (Liu et al., 2020).
text.formatted: However, a systematic review and meta-analysis found that passive and active SI share largely comparable clinical and psychological correlates, including associations with suicide attempts <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Liu et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: We extend this literature by suggesting that passive SI may arise not only in the context of defeat and entrapment but may also precede them.
Clinically, this raises the possibility that passive SI can be part of a selfreinforcing cycle of suicidal distress.
Assessment of passive SI may therefore provide an opportunity to identify and intervene on an unfolding cycle of suicidal distress, even in the absence of active thoughts of killing oneself.
Several limitations of the present study point to important directions for future research.
First, although EMA and the present analytic approach allowed us to establish temporal ordering over relatively short intervals, the observed prospective associations do not establish causality.
Moreover, the study focused on defeat and entrapment without repeatedly assessing several experiences that may precede or shape these states.
The IMV model situates defeat and entrapment within a broader framework that includes triggering events and experiences such as humiliation and failed social struggles (O'Connor & Kirtley, 2018).
text.formatted: The IMV model situates defeat and entrapment within a broader framework that includes triggering events and experiences such as humiliation and failed social struggles <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(O'Connor & Kirtley, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Future intensive longitudinal research could therefore assess these experiences alongside defeat, entrapment, and SI to test more complete pathways proposed by the model.
Examining specific daily-life events may be particularly informative.

Interpersonal setbacks, rejection or exclusion, conflict, and academic or occupational stressors are linked to suicide-related outcomes (Liu et al., 2014; Stewart et al., 2019; Stewart et al., 2024) and may be contexts in which perceptions of defeat and entrapment emerge.
text.formatted: Interpersonal setbacks, rejection or exclusion, conflict, and academic or occupational stressors are linked to suicide-related outcomes <ref type="bibr">(Liu et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Stewart et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Stewart et al., 2024)</ref> and may be contexts in which perceptions of defeat and entrapment emerge.

text.text: Measuring these contexts could clarify the circumstances that give rise to defeat and entrapment.
Second, the temporal relationships we identified occurred over the roughly three-hour interval between assessments.
Relationships among these constructs may operate differently across shorter or longer periods, and processes occurring between EMA assessments could not be captured.
This consideration is particularly important given evidence that suicidal thinking can fluctuate meaningfully within minutes (Coppersmith et al., 2023).
text.formatted: This consideration is particularly important given evidence that suicidal thinking can fluctuate meaningfully within minutes <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Coppersmith et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The reciprocal associations between defeat, entrapment, and passive SI observed here may characterize their relationship over several hours but may not necessarily emerge in the same way over minutes, days, or weeks.

Future studies using measurement-burst designs, with more frequent assessments during selected periods, could help determine whether defeat precedes entrapment over shorter intervals or whether reciprocal associations are evident even at these timescales.

Examining these processes across multiple timescales could provide a stronger test of whether the sequential pathway proposed by the IMV operates at some timescales while more reciprocal processes characterize others.
Third, our study could not establish whether defeat and entrapment contribute to the initial onset of SI because participants all had a recent history of SI and/or attempts.
Factors associated with changes in existing SI may not necessarily be the same factors that contribute to its first occurrence.

Future longitudinal research including individuals across a broader range of suicide histories could examine whether increases in defeat and entrapment precede the emergence of new-onset SI, fluctuations among individuals with established SI, or both.
Further, given the different prospective findings for passive and active SI, future research could examine within-person transitions between these forms of thinking.
Such work could help clarify whether defeat and entrapment play different roles in the emergence, maintenance, or changing content of suicidal thoughts over time.
Participants were young adults with a recent history of suicidal thoughts or behaviours, recruited from a university study pool and the broader community in Eastern Ontario, Canada.
Thus, findings may not generalize to adolescents, older adults, individuals without prior suicidal thoughts or behaviours, or clinical populations.
Developmental and contextual experiences may also influence how defeat and entrapment arise and relate to SI.

For example, interpersonal relationships, increasing independence, and academic or occupational transitions may be particularly relevant sources of defeat and entrapment during young adulthood (Arnett et al., 2014; Miller & Prinstein, 2019).
text.formatted: For example, interpersonal relationships, increasing independence, and academic or occupational transitions may be particularly relevant sources of defeat and entrapment during young adulthood <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Arnett et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Miller & Prinstein, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings may be limited by the measures and assessment procedures used.
We assessed defeat and entrapment using brief adaptations of established measures (Griffiths et al., 2015), whereas we assessed passive and active SI using a single item each.
text.formatted: We assessed defeat and entrapment using brief adaptations of established measures <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Griffiths et al., 2015)</ref>, whereas we assessed passive and active SI using a single item each.

text.text: Different measures or operationalizations of these constructs may yield different associations.
Moreover, the temporal relationships observed here reflect approximately three-hour assessment intervals over 21 days.

We expect repeated assessments in naturalistic settings to be important for capturing these within-person associations, although the specific smartphone application or survey delivery platform is unlikely to be essential.
Whether similar patterns generalize to different assessment intervals, measurement approaches, and populations is an open question.
Are participants were predominantly women and White, although several other gender and racial or ethnic groups were represented.
Recruitment from a university study pool and the surrounding community influenced this composition.

We cannot determine whether the observed associations would generalize to other demographic groups; further research with more diverse samples is needed to establish whether these apply to diverse gender, racial, and ethnic identities.
We conducted a temporally fine-grained examination of relationships between defeat, entrapment, and SI in daily life.
Our findings support the motivational phase of the IMV model while also suggesting a more complex pattern than a strictly sequential pathway from defeat to entrapment to SI.
Defeat and entrapment were reciprocally associated over time, and both predicted subsequent increases in passive and active SI.
However, these relationships were also reciprocal for passive SI, though not for active SI.

Together, these findings highlight the value of examining suicide-related processes within individuals over short timescales while also considering meaningful differences in the content of suicidal thoughts.

Situating these proximal processes within the broader interpersonal, developmental, and contextual experiences in which they occur may provide a more complete understanding of how suicidal thinking develops and changes.
